about: ONE table of owner vectors for common/test-leftovers.md section 3, run against BOTH implementations by tools/owner-conformance.test.mjs: owner_ok()/liveness() in tools/janitor.sh and parseOwner()/ownerState() in tools/lib/owned.mjs. Data only: nothing here is a test. Hosts are examples; no real machine names.

grammar.about: text is the content of an owner file or a lock reason as the reader sees it. valid=true means rule section 3's `<host>@<os>:<pid>[:<start>]` accepts it; valid=false means 'not exactly the form' (so the verdict is unknown, never gone). The rule fixes: host = no '@', no ':', no whitespace; os = exactly linux|macos|windows (lower case); pid and start = decimal digits; start optional; one line.

verdicts.about: owner + facts -> live | gone | unknown, per section 3's liveness procedure. host: same | same-case (this machine's name with the case swapped: compared case-insensitively) | foreign-name | foreign-os (this machine's name, another os tag: a Windows machine and its WSL share one name and have two pid spaces). pid: absent (no such process) | present | refused (the liveness query failed or was refused). startDelta: null = the owner carries no start, else owner.start - live start in seconds. liveStart: whether the reader can read the live process's start. pidText replaces the generated unmatchable pid with a literal pid text. ownerText replaces the generated owner with raw text ({HOST} = this machine's `<name>@<os>`, {NAME} = its name). tasklist=true: the vector also runs through the janitor's Windows branch (a stubbed tasklist), a representative subset because every janitor run spawns many processes. sides: which implementation can express the vector; the janitor never reads a start, so a vector whose verdict depends on a MISMATCH of two starts is node-only (section 3 lets a reader that cannot read the live start answer live); for those the janitor is held only to the safety property: it must not delete.

alive, starts 3 s apart: a reused pid or a stepped clock, never proof of death and never proof of life

pid 0 is digits (the grammar takes it) but names no process; a pid that cannot be a process says nothing, so it is never 'gone' (the 'no such process' answer is about a real pid that nothing holds). The stub ps answers 'no such process' for it, as ps -p 0 does on Linux

on Windows a bash started by a native process reports pid 1 for itself and its parent, and Windows has no pid 1: the process list has no row and process.kill says ESRCH, so a live CI job whose owner pid was taken from $PPID would read as gone. Pid 1 on a windows owner is unknown. (On any other machine this owner is another host's.)
a 25-digit pid cannot name a process and is not a safe integer; same reasoning as v23

windows-owner.about: token is the Windows owner of an account name, rule section 1: the account name without its domain (a domain-qualified name is not an input; the bare name is), the ASCII letters A-Z lower-cased and nothing else changed, encoded as UTF-8 (the bytes of the name alone, NO line end: printf '%s' in bash, never echo), hashed with SHA-256, the first four bytes of the digest read as a big-endian unsigned 32-bit integer, written in decimal without leading zeros (1 to 10 digits), behind the letter w. A hash collision confers no authority: the file's owner decides.

an upper-case letter is lower-cased first: Alice and alice are one account

a space is part of the name and is hashed as it is (a Windows account name may hold one)
a multi-byte letter: the UTF-8 bytes of the name are hashed; only ASCII A-Z is lower-cased
the capital Ø is NOT lower-cased (ASCII only), so this is another token than søren
the same bytes as Søren: only the ASCII S changed

a different token from Ünal, for the same reason
dots and hyphens are part of the name
the shortest name

a plain name whose digest starts with a byte >= 0x80, so the token is >= 2^31: a signed 32-bit read would print a negative number, a 64-bit unsigned one the table's value (bash `$(( 16#… ))` and Node `readUInt32BE` must both give it)

record.about: text is the content of a claim file or a lock reason of the MERGED record, rule section 3: <owner>:<host>@<os>:<pid>[:<start>[:<ns>]] with owner ^[uw][0-9]{1,10}$. valid=true means the grammar accepts it. The vectors of the grammar table (before the owner segment) appear here behind an owner field with their verdict unchanged; that table stays as the LEGACY grammar <host>@<os>:<pid>[:<start>] in which a legacy name's record is read.

scope.about: Facts for ownerState of the MERGED record (rule section 3). nameOwner is the owner segment of the resource's name, recordOwner the first field of its record, callerOwner the caller's token, kernelMine whether the kernel owner of the resource is the caller (a file the caller does not own is no evidence), ns is the record's pid namespace against the reader's (same | absent | other; only a Linux reader requires one), pid is absent (no such process: the one answer that can mean gone), present or refused, hidepid says the process list may hide other users' processes. expected is gone | live | unknown. The host is always this machine's.
